blocks.text: A car body panel, a locomotive axle and a woodworking chisel are all 'steel', yet a panel can be pressed into a deep curve, an axle can take millions of load cycles and a chisel can hold a razor edge. The three differ mainly in how much carbon they contain and which alloying elements are added; learning the classification tells you what to expect before you open a data sheet.

blocks.markdown: Steel is iron with carbon (up to about 2.1 wt%) and usually manganese and other alloying elements. At room temperature carbon is mostly in the compound iron carbide (cementite, Fe$_3$C). In slowly cooled steel, the microstructure is **ferrite** (soft, ductile, nearly pure iron) and **pearlite** (a lamellar mixture of ferrite and cementite, stronger and harder), and the proportion of pearlite rises with carbon content up to 0.76 wt% C, the eutectoid composition.

blocks.title: Plain carbon and alloy steels
blocks.text: A **plain carbon steel** contains carbon, up to about 1 % manganese and small residual impurities, and no deliberate additions. An **alloy steel** has additional elements (Cr, Ni, Mo, V, Mn above about 1 %) added to change hardenability, toughness, strength at temperature or corrosion resistance. Boundaries between classes vary between authors; the values below are typical.

rows: Ductile, tough, readily formed and welded; cannot be hardened much by quenching
Car body sheet, structural sections, pipes, bolts
Ferrite and a larger fraction of pearlite
Stronger; responds well to quenching and tempering; less weldable
Springs, cutting tools, wire, chisels, rails (pearlitic steels of about 0.7 to 0.8 % C)
blocks.caption: Classification of carbon steels by carbon content.
Lever rule just below the eutectoid temperature: C0 is the carbon content in wt%, 0.022 wt% the carbon in ferrite at the eutectoid temperature and 0.76 wt% the eutectoid composition (all in wt% C).

blocks.title: Microstructure of a low-carbon steel
blocks.prompt: A 0.20 wt% C steel is cooled slowly from the austenite region. Find the fractions of pearlite and ferrite, and comment on the expected properties.

steps.text: The remainder is ferrite (this ferrite is the proeutectoid ferrite that forms first plus the ferrite in the pearlite).
Interpretation: with only about 24 % pearlite the steel is mostly ferrite, so it is soft and ductile with moderate strength, consistent with a mild structural or sheet steel.

blocks.answer: About 24 % pearlite and 76 % ferrite: a ductile, weldable low-carbon steel.

blocks.markdown: **Alloying elements.** Alloying elements are added to steel for four main reasons: to increase **hardenability** (the depth to which a steel can be hardened by quenching), to improve toughness, to retain strength at high temperature, and to resist corrosion.

rows: Raises hardenability and wear resistance by forming carbides; above about 10.5 % gives a passive oxide film and corrosion resistance (stainless steel); stabilises ferrite
Stabilises austenite (so austenitic stainless is non-magnetic and tough at low temperature); raises toughness and low-temperature impact strength; modest hardenability
Strongly raises hardenability; resists temper embrittlement and creep at high temperature; improves pitting resistance in stainless steels
Combines with sulphur to form MnS and prevents brittle iron sulphide at grain boundaries (hot shortness); deoxidises; raises hardenability and strength; stabilises austenite at high content
blocks.caption: Roles of four common alloying elements.

IIW carbon equivalent, with all contents in wt%. A higher CE means a greater tendency to form hard martensite in a weld heat-affected zone and a lower weldability; steels with CE below about 0.4 are generally easy to weld (typical guidance).

blocks.title: Carbon equivalent of an alloy steel
blocks.prompt: A structural alloy steel has (in wt%) C 0.20, Mn 1.20, Cr 0.50, Mo 0.10, Ni 0.30, and no V or Cu. Calculate the carbon equivalent and comment on its weldability.

steps.text: Evaluate each group in the formula.
Add the contributions to the carbon.
Interpretation: at 0.54 the steel is above the easy-welding guideline of about 0.4, so preheating or controlled heat input is needed to avoid hard, brittle martensite in the heat-affected zone.

blocks.answer: CE = 0.54; the steel is hardenable and needs careful welding procedure (preheat).

blocks.markdown: **Austenitic stainless steel.** The usual grades contain about 18 wt% chromium and 8 to 10 wt% nickel, with low carbon (typically under 0.08 %). The nickel stabilises the face-centred cubic austenite structure down to room temperature, so the steel is non-magnetic, very ductile and tough even at cryogenic temperatures, and it work-hardens rapidly. It cannot be hardened by quenching. The chromium forms a thin, self-healing chromium-oxide passive film ($\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$) as long as there is enough oxygen and the chromium content in solid solution stays above about 10.5 wt%.

rows: Austenitic; general-purpose; vulnerable to chloride pitting
Austenitic; Mo improves pitting resistance in chloride
Martensitic; hardenable by quenching, moderate corrosion resistance
blocks.caption: Representative stainless steel grades; compositions are typical ranges.

blocks.title: Sensitisation (weld decay) and chloride attack
blocks.text: If an austenitic stainless steel is held between about 450 and 850 C (for example in a weld heat-affected zone), chromium carbide ($\mathrm{Cr_{23}C_6}$) precipitates at grain boundaries and removes chromium from the adjacent metal, which falls below 10.5 % and loses its passive film; intergranular corrosion follows. Remedies are low-carbon grades (304L), stabilised grades (321, 347, containing Ti or Nb that tie up carbon) or solution annealing. Austenitic grades also suffer pitting and stress-corrosion cracking in warm chloride solutions; molybdenum (316) improves but does not remove the risk.

points: Carbon content classifies steel: low (below about 0.25 %) is ductile and weldable, medium (about 0.25 to 0.6 %) is heat-treatable, and high (above about 0.6 %) is hard and wear resistant; pearlite fraction rises as $(C_0-0.022)/(0.76-0.022)$.

Cr gives hardenability and, above about 10.5 %, corrosion resistance; Ni stabilises austenite and gives toughness; Mo raises hardenability and creep and pitting resistance; Mn ties up sulphur and raises hardenability and strength.
Austenitic stainless steel (about 18 % Cr, 8 to 10 % Ni) is non-magnetic and ductile and resists corrosion through a Cr2O3 film, but is vulnerable to sensitisation and chloride attack.

questions.stem: A steel contains 0.45 wt% C and is slowly cooled. How is it classified, and what is a typical application?

options.text: Low carbon steel, suitable for deep-drawn car body panels
High carbon steel, suitable for cutting tools
Medium carbon steel, suitable for shafts and axles that are quenched and tempered
Stainless steel, suitable for food equipment

questions.correctOptionText: Medium carbon steel, suitable for shafts and axles that are quenched and tempered

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: low-carbon steels have under about 0.25 wt% C.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: high-carbon steels have over about 0.6 wt% C.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: 0.45 wt% C lies in the medium-carbon range, which responds well to heat treatment and is used for shafts and axles.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: stainless steels are defined by their chromium content, not by carbon alone.

questions.explanation: Carbon steels are classified as low (below about 0.25 %), medium (about 0.25 to 0.6 %) and high (above about 0.6 %). A 0.45 % steel has enough carbon to be hardened by quenching and tempered to give a strong, tough shaft or axle.

questions.stem: Why is a low-carbon steel with about 0.1 wt% C preferred for pressed car body panels?

options.text: It is mostly ferrite, so it is ductile, formable, weldable and cheap
It is mostly cementite, so it is hard and wear resistant
It can be quenched to a very hard martensitic structure after pressing
It contains 18 % chromium and resists corrosion

questions.correctOptionText: It is mostly ferrite, so it is ductile, formable, weldable and cheap

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the ferrite-rich microstructure gives high ductility, formability and weldability at low cost.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: a low-carbon steel contains little cementite.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: very low carbon prevents it from hardening much on quenching, which suits forming and welding.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: plain low-carbon steel has no chromium; corrosion protection is by coating.

questions.explanation: At 0.1 % C the slowly cooled structure is mostly soft ferrite with about 11 % pearlite. That gives the ductility needed for deep drawing and good weldability, and the steel is protected from rust by paint or zinc coating.

questions.stem: What is the main reason for adding nickel to an austenitic stainless steel?

options.text: It forms hard carbides that give wear resistance
It ties up sulphur as nickel sulphide
It is the element responsible for the passive oxide film
It stabilises the austenite structure at room temperature, giving a non-magnetic, tough and ductile steel

questions.correctOptionText: It stabilises the austenite structure at room temperature, giving a non-magnetic, tough and ductile steel

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: carbide formation is the role of chromium, molybdenum and vanadium.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: sulphur is tied up by manganese as MnS.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the passive film is chromium oxide.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: nickel is an austenite stabiliser, so the FCC structure persists to low temperatures.

questions.explanation: Iron is FCC (austenite) only at high temperature; nickel extends the austenite field down to room temperature and below. This gives the non-magnetic, ductile, tough behaviour of grades such as 304 and 316.

questions.stem: What is the main role of manganese in most carbon and alloy steels?

options.text: It forms the protective oxide film that prevents rusting
It combines with sulphur to form MnS, preventing brittle iron sulphide, and it raises strength and hardenability
It lowers the carbon content of the steel
It is added solely to make the steel non-magnetic

questions.correctOptionText: It combines with sulphur to form MnS, preventing brittle iron sulphide, and it raises strength and hardenability

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the protective oxide film on stainless steel comes from chromium.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: Mn avoids hot shortness by tying up sulphur as MnS, and it also increases hardenability.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: manganese does not reduce the carbon content.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: non-magnetic behaviour requires austenite stabilisation, usually by nickel.

questions.explanation: Sulphur forms low-melting iron sulphide at grain boundaries that causes hot shortness. Manganese has a higher affinity for sulphur and forms harmless MnS particles, and it also deoxidises the melt and raises hardenability.

questions.stem: What gives 18 wt% Cr, 8 wt% Ni austenitic stainless steel its corrosion resistance, and what is the limit?

options.text: A thick layer of nickel oxide that blocks all ions
A coating of zinc that sacrifices itself
Its high carbon content that forms a hard surface
A thin self-healing Cr2O3 film that needs enough chromium in solid solution (above about 10.5 %) and oxygen

questions.correctOptionText: A thin self-healing Cr2O3 film that needs enough chromium in solid solution (above about 10.5 %) and oxygen

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: nickel stabilises austenite but is not the passive film.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: stainless steels are not zinc coated; the film forms from the alloy itself.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: low carbon is preferred; carbon can precipitate chromium carbide and reduce corrosion resistance.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the chromium-oxide film forms when chromium exceeds about 10.5 % and heals in the presence of oxygen.

questions.explanation: Chromium reacts with oxygen to form a thin Cr2O3 film that stops further attack and re-forms if damaged. The film depends on there being more than about 10.5 % chromium in solid solution; if it is locally depleted, as in sensitised steel, the passive film fails.

questions.stem: A 0.55 wt% C steel is cooled slowly from the austenite region. Using the lever rule with 0.022 wt% C in ferrite and a eutectoid composition of 0.76 wt% C, find the mass percentage of pearlite in the microstructure.
questions.explanation: The fraction of pearlite is $(0.55-0.022)/(0.76-0.022)=0.528/0.738=0.715$. So 71.5 % of the microstructure is pearlite and the rest is ferrite, which explains why a medium-carbon steel is much stronger than a mild steel.

questions.stem: A low-alloy steel contains, in wt%, C 0.18, Mn 1.40, Cr 0.30, Mo 0.20 and Ni 0.60, with no V or Cu. Calculate the IIW carbon equivalent $\mathrm{CE}=C+Mn/6+(Cr+Mo+V)/5+(Ni+Cu)/15$. Give a dimensionless value.
questions.explanation: The terms are $Mn/6=0.2333$, $(Cr+Mo+V)/5=0.50/5=0.100$ and $(Ni+Cu)/15=0.60/15=0.040$. Adding to the carbon gives $\mathrm{CE}=0.18+0.2333+0.100+0.040=0.553$, so this steel is a rather hardenable grade that needs care in welding.

questions.stem: A batch of 800 kg of austenitic stainless steel contains 8.0 wt% nickel. Calculate the mass of nickel in the batch, in kg.
questions.explanation: The mass of nickel is the mass fraction times the batch mass, $0.080\times800=64$ kg. A typical 304 melt would also contain about 18 to 20 % chromium, about 144 to 160 kg in the same batch.

questions.stem: Explain why an austenitic stainless steel can suffer intergranular corrosion after welding, and describe two ways to prevent it. State the role of chromium in the corrosion resistance of the steel.
markingGuide: Chromium gives a passive Cr2O3 film when above about 10.5 % in solid solution
Holding between about 450 and 850 C in the heat-affected zone allows Cr23C6 to precipitate at grain boundaries
Chromium near the boundary is depleted below about 10.5 %, so the passive film fails there (sensitisation)
Corrosion follows the grain boundaries (weld decay)
Prevention: low-carbon grade (304L), stabilised grade with Ti or Nb (321, 347), or solution annealing and quenching after welding
The rest of the grain is unaffected because it still has enough chromium
questions.explanation: Carbide precipitation consumes chromium locally, and corrosion resistance depends on the local chromium content. Preventing carbide formation or fixing the carbon with a stabiliser keeps the chromium in solution.

questions.stem: Select a steel (class and any alloying additions) for each of (i) a deep-drawn car door panel, (ii) a heavily loaded crankshaft and (iii) a hand chisel that must hold a hard edge. Justify each choice using the carbon content and the role of the alloying elements Cr, Ni, Mo or Mn.
markingGuide: (i) Low-carbon steel (under about 0.25 % C, mostly ferrite): ductile, formable, weldable, cheap
(ii) Medium-carbon steel (about 0.4 % C), quenched and tempered, with Mn and perhaps Cr and Mo to raise hardenability, and Mo to resist temper embrittlement; Ni for toughness if needed
(iii) High-carbon steel (about 0.7 to 1.0 % C), hardened and tempered, giving a hard, wear-resistant edge; Cr to raise hardenability and form hard carbides
States that higher carbon raises hardness and strength but lowers ductility and weldability
Mentions Mn tying up sulphur as MnS in all three, or the role of each element correctly
questions.explanation: Carbon content sets the basic strength-ductility balance, and alloying elements fine-tune hardenability, toughness and wear resistance. The three components lie at different points on the carbon scale for that reason.
